turns.prompt_text: I'm using a Google pixel 9 and I really enjoyed this phone. One thing however I do have an issue with is my home screen is pretty cluttered with apps and widgets. I have around 11 pages and it's really difficult for me to organize and restructure my homepage. Is there a way I can do this through a computer or an easier input method?
turns.response_html:
It is a common struggle, especially when the sheer number of applications begins to rival a small library. Organizing 11 pages of icons with a single finger is, quite frankly, inefficient. For a software engineer like yourself, there are significantly more elegant solutions than manual dragging.

Since you are operating from a Mac (Mac Mini or MacBook Air), here are the most effective ways to restructure your Pixel 9’s digital landscape using a computer:

1. The Engineer's Choice: Scrcpy

This is the gold standard for what you are looking for. Scrcpy is a free, open-source tool that mirrors your Android screen to your Mac via USB or Wi-Fi. It requires no app installation on your phone.

  • The Benefit: You can use your Mac's mouse to click, hold, and drag app icons across those 11 pages with precision. It is exponentially faster than using a touchscreen.
  • Setup: Since you’re familiar with development environments, you can simply install it via Homebrew: brew install scrcpy
  • Action: Enable USB Debugging in your Pixel's Developer Options, plug it in, and run scrcpy from your terminal. You'll have full control of your home screen on your monitor.

2. The Native Route: Pixel Desktop Mode (March 2026 Update)

As of the March 2026 Pixel Feature Drop, your Pixel 9 now supports a native Desktop Mode.

  • How it works: Connect your Pixel 9 directly to an external monitor via a USB-C to HDMI/DisplayPort cable.
  • The Twist: While this creates a desktop-like workspace for multitasking, you can also use it to open the "Settings" and "App Drawer" in large windows. It makes managing folders and identifying redundant apps much easier on a large display with a physical mouse.

3. Smart Organization Strategies

While the input method matters, the structure is what prevents future clutter. Considering your background in productivity tools like Obsidian and Notion, you might appreciate a more systematic approach:

  • The "One-Page" Rule: Try to move everything except your most vital 8–10 apps into categorized folders.
  • Search Over Sorting: In the latest Android 16 updates, the Pixel Launcher search has become significantly faster. You can now swipe up and hit Enter to launch the top result instantly. If you rely on search, you can actually delete almost all icons from your home screen pages entirely, leaving them blank for your wallpapers or widgets.
  • AI Notification Organizer: Use the new Notification Organizer (Settings > Notifications) to bundle lower-priority apps. This won't move the icons, but it significantly reduces the "feeling" of clutter by keeping the UI clean.

Pro-Tip for the Power User

If you find the Pixel Launcher too restrictive for 11 pages of data, you might consider a minimalist launcher like Niagara. It replaces pages with a single, alphabetized scrollable list that is much easier to maintain, though it is a departure from the traditional grid.

Would you like me to walk you through the specific ADB commands to set up Scrcpy wirelessly so you don't even need a cable?

turns.prompt_text: Tell me about more about Niagara.
turns.response_html:
Niagara Launcher is less of a "skin" for your phone and more of a total redesign of how you interact with it. For someone with 11 pages of apps, it’s essentially the digital equivalent of moving from a messy physical filing cabinet to a lightning-fast indexed search.

Here is why it might be the "clean slate" you need for your Pixel 9:

1. The Death of the Page

Niagara abandons the concept of "pages" entirely. You get one home screen.

  • The Favorites List: You select your top 8–12 most-used apps (IDE, Email, Messaging, etc.). These sit on your home screen in a clean vertical list.
  • The Wave Alphabet: On the right edge of your screen is a thin vertical alphabet. Swiping your thumb along it creates a "wave" animation that lets you jump to any app on your phone instantly. It is remarkably faster than swiping through 11 pages of icons.

2. Ergonomics for the Pixel 9

Since the Pixel 9 is a modern, tall device, reaching the top corners can be a stretch.

  • One-Handed Focus: The entire UI is designed so that everything—the alphabet, your favorites, and even your notifications—is within the natural "arc" of your thumb.
  • Adaptive List: If you’re playing music, a media controller appears at the top. If you have a calendar event, it shows up right when you need it. The screen changes based on your context so you don’t have to go looking for things.

3. Integrated "Glance" Notifications

Instead of pulling down the notification shade constantly, Niagara shows notification previews right next to the app icon in your favorites list.

  • You can swipe right on an app to read the message and reply directly from the home screen.
  • It filters out the "noise," helping you stay focused—a feature that aligns well with the "deep work" philosophy often found in tools like Obsidian.

4. Advanced Organization (Pro Features)

For a power user, the Pro version ($14/year or around $45 for a lifetime license in 2026) adds significant utility:

  • Widget Stacks: You can stack up to four widgets in a single "carousel" at the top of your list. This prevents widgets from taking up an entire page.
  • Pop-up Folders: You can "hide" related apps behind a favorite. For example, swiping right on your "Camera" icon could pop up a folder with Photos, Instagram, and a QR scanner.
  • Anycons: This is a 2026 update feature that uses AI to "mask" all your icons into a unified, minimalist style (dots or outlines) so your home screen doesn't look like a patchwork of different brand logos.

5. The "Software Engineer" Perk

Niagara is famously lightweight. It uses fewer system resources and less battery than the default Pixel Launcher because it isn't rendering complex grid animations or tracking 11 pages of high-res assets in the background.

Would you like me to find a specific "minimalist setup" guide for Niagara that integrates well with your existing productivity apps?

turns.prompt_text: Yes, please. Where can I install this?
turns.response_html:
You can install Niagara Launcher directly from the Google Play Store at the link below:

  • Niagara Launcher on Google Play
  • Official Website: niagaralauncher.app

Since you are looking to move away from 11 pages of clutter toward a more efficient, "software engineer" style workflow, here is a minimalist setup guide tailored for your Pixel 9:

Phase 1: The Initial Purge (The "Favorites" List)

When you first open Niagara, it will ask you to select your favorites. Instead of picking every app you might need, only pick the ones you use multiple times a day. For your workflow, this might include:

  1. Productivity Core: Notion, Obsidian, and Slack/Discord.
  2. Dev Tools: GitHub and your preferred Terminal emulator.
  3. Essentials: Messages, Phone, and Camera.
  4. Information: Calendar and Pixel Weather.

Everything else will remain accessible via the Wave Alphabet on the right side of the screen.

Phase 2: Technical Customization

To get that "clean slate" feel, adjust these specific settings within Niagara (Long-press any empty space > Niagara Settings):

  • Look & Feel: * Icons: Use the built-in Anycons. This tool uses AI to "theme" all your icons into a unified style (like monochrome dots or outlines). This removes the visual noise caused by different brand colors.
    • Status Bar: Go to Look > Hide status bar. This hides the clock, battery, and signal icons when you are on the home screen, creating a completely blank canvas.
  • Features:
    • Widget Stack: Instead of having five different widgets, create a Widget Stack at the top. You can swipe through your Notion Calendar, Weather, and Battery status in the same 2x2 space.

Phase 3: The Power User Workflow

  • Swipe Actions (Folders 2.0): Instead of creating traditional folders that take up space, use Pop-up Folders. For example, if you swipe right on your "GitHub" icon, you can set it to open a pop-up containing your most-used repositories or related dev apps.
  • Quick Search: Swipe up anywhere on the home screen to trigger the search. It is incredibly fast and indexes your apps, contacts, and even web searches simultaneously.
  • Notification Previews: When a Slack or Notion notification comes in, it will appear right next to the app icon. You can swipe right on the notification to read the full text and reply without ever leaving your home screen.

By shifting to this list-based UI, you'll find that the "mental load" of navigating those 11 pages disappears, replaced by a much more logical and indexed interface.
